clue.text: "Out of the ash I rise with my red hair And I –." (Sylvia Plath)

definitions.text: "Out of the ash I rise with my red hair And I –."
definitions.meaning: the surface reading: a line of verse with its ending missing
the setter's reading: the gap is filled from the closing line of Plath's poem Lady Lazarus

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: there is no wordplay, and the solver must know or infer the last words of Plath's poem Lady Lazarus, where the speaker rises like a phoenix.
explanation.definitionFit: These four words complete the final line of Lady Lazarus, written by Plath in 1962 and published in Ariel.

clue.text: Estimator going around Luis Cardoso's home

indicators.note: something going around moves in circles and ends up in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who makes estimates is travelling round a writer's house.
explanation.walkthrough: Luis Cardoso is a novelist born in Portuguese Timor, the island territory now independent as Timor-Leste.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardoso was born and raised in this Southeast Asian nation, so it is fairly called his homeland.

clue.text: Passage author of The Land Downstairs read aloud

indicators.note: reading something out means we judge it by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: the surname of the writer of that book

explanation.surface: A section of a book by a certain author is being recited.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer's surname Tripp and the four-letter answer TRIP sound identical; only the doubled final consonant differs on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A passage can mean a journey or crossing, as in booking passage on a ship, which is a trip.

clue.text: Collections of hams picked to work well together?

definitions.meaning: the surface reading: assortments of cured pork legs, as in a butcher's selection
the setter's reading: hams are overacting performers, and companies of actors are cast to play as one unit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hams' looks like meat, but in theatre slang a ham is a showy, overacting performer; the question mark flags the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Groups of performers chosen to act or play as a coordinated company carry this name in theatre and music.

clue.text: Fish hooker boxes India for Pulitzer novelist

indicators.note: to box something is to pack it inside a case, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: an angler's bait with a hook, used to catch fish
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A fish-catching device encloses a country to serve an award-winning author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish hooker' reads like a person who fishes, but it describes the bait-and-hook device itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Alison Lurie won the 1985 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction with her novel Foreign Affairs.

clue.text: Jokes about religious type? Meg March has three of them

definitions.text: Meg March has three of them

indicators.note: one thing placed about another surrounds it on every side

parts.note: to kid is to joke or tease
a nun is addressed as Sister

explanation.surface: Gags about nuns, and a remark about a character in a famous novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Meg is the eldest of the four March girls in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women; Jo, Beth and Amy are all younger.
explanation.definitionFit: Younger female siblings are informally called this, and the eldest March girl has exactly three.

clue.text: Walker going round cold island, tucking into beer

indicators.note: tucking something into a space places it inside an enclosure

parts.note: ale is a type of beer

indicators.note: going round turns something to face the opposite way

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A hiker circles a chilly island before settling into a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walker' looks like a hiker, but it is the surname of the American novelist who wrote The Color Purple.
explanation.definitionFit: The author's first name is clued by her surname, a common trick for writers with very familiar names.

clue.text: To some, Reuben J. adds nothing to a list of names.

indicators.note: adding one thing to another here means slipping it in among the existing letters

parts.note: a roster is a list of people on duty
nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A man called Reuben J. contributes nothing to a register.
explanation.walkthrough: Reuben J. Cogburn is the marshal in Charles Portis's novel True Grit, known to almost everyone by his nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Cogburn is called by this nickname by those around him, so to some people that is his name.

clue.text: Cricket club president who knocked the butcher boy out?

definitions.text: who knocked the butcher boy out?

parts.note: the Marylebone Cricket Club, which owns Lord's in London
Abe Lincoln, the US president

explanation.surface: A sports club official who once floored a young meat-shop worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked out' sounds like a punch, but here it means produced in a hurry: Patrick McCabe wrote the novel The Butcher Boy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish novelist Patrick McCabe published The Butcher Boy in 1992, so he is its author.

clue.text: Western ninjitsu is sacrilegious, holds assassin

indicators.note: in an across entry, heading west means reading from right to left
a phrase that holds something keeps it inside, within its run of letters

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the end of the first word, the second word, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A comment that Western martial arts are irreverent and contain a killer.
explanation.walkthrough: Cassius is the conspirator who leads the plot against Caesar in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaius Cassius Longinus was one of the senators who stabbed Julius Caesar to death in 44 BC.

clue.text: Staff turn around state opera about Spanish king

indicators.note: to sit around something is to surround it on both sides

parts.note: a rod is a staff or stick
a go is a turn in a game
RI is the postal abbreviation for Rhode Island

explanation.surface: Staff turn their backs on a state-funded opera about a Spanish monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn around' looks like one phrase meaning reverse; it splits into a noun and the surrounding signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Handel's early Italian opera Rodrigo concerns Roderic, the last Visigothic king of Spain.

clue.text: Husbandless writer that's run off with King's Christine

indicators.note: whatever has gone off has departed, so it is dropped from the word

parts.note: a writer is an author, and H, the abbreviation for husband, is left out
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A writer with no husband has eloped with a woman called Christine.
explanation.walkthrough: AUTHOR loses its H and then its R. Christine is the possessed car in Stephen King's novel of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Christine is a murderous 1958 Plymouth Fury, and auto is a common word for a motor car.

clue.text: Budd's problem? Timid men at sea hampering training

indicators.note: to hamper is to get in the way, so this piece sits in the middle
someone at sea is confused and disordered

parts.note: taken as written
PE is physical education, school sports training

explanation.surface: A naval story: nervous sailors getting in the way of drill.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Budd, in Melville's novella, has a stammer that leaves him speechless when accused, and he strikes out instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A speech defect such as a stammer is called a speech impediment, which was Budd's fatal flaw.

clue.text: Push a chap and he'll go to the papers for publicity

definitions.text: he'll go to the papers for publicity

parts.note: to press is to push
taken as written
a gent is a gentleman or chap

explanation.surface: Lean on a man and he will run to the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a threat of a leak; the definition is a job description.
explanation.definitionFit: A publicist employed to get stories about a client printed in newspapers is known by this title.

clue.text: Her mate had the hump about son's green article

indicators.note: one piece placed about another wraps round it

parts.note: emerald is a shade of green
S is the abbreviation for son
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A woman's husband sulked over their son's environmental essay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had the hump' is British slang for being in a bad mood, but here it is literal: Quasimodo, the hunchback of Notre-Dame, adores her.
explanation.definitionFit: In Victor Hugo's novel the gypsy dancer is loved by the hunchbacked bell-ringer Quasimodo, her devoted companion.

clue.text: No-good culinary art that Trillian must have studied

indicators.note: no means without, so this letter must be removed

parts.note: gastronomy is the art of fine cooking and eating
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A useless kind of cookery that a certain character must have learned.
explanation.walkthrough: Trillian, in Douglas Adams's The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, has a degree in maths and a doctorate in astrophysics.
explanation.definitionFit: Her astrophysics doctorate implies study of the science of stars and planets.

clue.text: Posh party held in empty tower of Wolf Hall house?

indicators.note: to be held in something is to be enclosed by it
an emptied word keeps only its shell, with its middle gone

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
U stands for upper-class, a British label for posh usage
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A smart party takes place in an abandoned tower at a stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' looks like a building, but it is a royal dynasty: Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall is set at Henry VIII's court.
explanation.definitionFit: The ruling dynasty of Henry VIII is a royal house in the genealogical sense, and Wolf Hall depicts it.

clue.text: Injured bicep, case for eager Dr. Finlay?

indicators.note: something injured is damaged and bent out of shape

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only its outer letters count

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
the abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A damaged arm muscle makes a fitting case for a keen television doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Finlay was a Scottish TV doctor; but the Booker-winning author of Vernon God Little was born Peter Finlay and writes as DBC Pierre.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist's birth name is Peter Warren Finlay, so this pen name and Finlay are the same person.

clue.text: Poet said to have a share of cakes jammed by queen

indicators.note: something jammed by another is wedged tightly inside it

parts.note: a few cakes, a portion of a batch, are buns
R is Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A poet is supposed to get some cakes with jam made by royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet, called his country the 'Land o' Cakes', which gives the surface its joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns is the celebrated eighteenth-century Scottish poet behind Auld Lang Syne and Tam o' Shanter.

clue.text: Take property up: unfinished flat in Ruxton Towers?

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: to rob is to take someone's property

indicators.note: something unfinished stops short of its last letter

parts.note: flat beer or bread has gone stale

explanation.surface: A property dispute over a half-built apartment in a grand building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment but means stale. Ruxton Towers is the youth detention centre in Alan Sillitoe's The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner.
explanation.definitionFit: A borstal was a British reform institution for young offenders, the kind of place Sillitoe's runner is held.

clue.text: LIke Vanity Fair to transcribe CIA trials?

indicators.note: transcribing rewrites material in another form, here a new letter order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A glossy magazine writing up spy agency court cases.
explanation.walkthrough: Vanity Fair here is Thackeray's novel, a mocking portrait of English society, not the magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's novel ridicules social climbing and greed, so it is a work of mocking social criticism.

clue.text: Supporter gripped by French article on United pen

indicators.note: to be gripped is to be held tightly inside something

parts.note: le is French for the
U is the abbreviation for United in football team names
a fan supports a team

explanation.surface: A football fan grips a French newspaper article about Manchester United.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a writing tool or an enclosure, but stands for a writer: Sheridan Le Fanu, the Irish author of Carmilla.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen is crossword shorthand for a writer, and Le Fanu wrote Victorian Gothic fiction.

clue.text: Novelist in print cooking radish and corn

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, mixing them into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A published writer is making a dish of vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Richardson, author of Pamela and Clarissa, was by trade a London printer.
explanation.definitionFit: Richardson ran a printing business as well as writing novels, so he was a novelist in the print trade.

clue.text: A collector of extremely colourful Faberge work?

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
Fabergé is famous for jewelled eggs made for the Russian tsars

explanation.surface: Someone who collects bright Fabergé pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A collector' reads as anyone who collects; it is the butterfly-collecting kidnapper in John Fowles's The Collector.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederick Clegg is the title character of Fowles's novel, so he is literally that book's collector.

clue.text: Grumpy daughter bitter about about Beowulf's ending

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter

indicators.note: about means turned around, and the doubled word looks like a misprint for a single one

parts.note: a bitter wind is a raw one

indicators.note: an ending is the final part, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the hero of the Old English epic poem

explanation.surface: A sulky daughter complains about the end of the Old English epic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grumpy' looks like an adjective describing the daughter, but it is the name of one of Snow White's seven companions.
explanation.definitionFit: Grumpy is one of the seven small miners in the Disney Snow White, an example of the category.

clue.text: A female accompanied by religious singer

indicators.note: being accompanied means having company placed alongside, one piece next to another

parts.note: pi is short for pious
taken as written
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A woman goes with a devout vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: PI for pious is a crossword staple. Édith Piaf was the French singer of Non, je ne regrette rien.
explanation.definitionFit: Édith Piaf was France's most celebrated chanteuse, so she is a famous example of a vocalist.

clue.text: Gaston's lover seeing lasses, both half-cut

indicators.note: half-cut means each word loses half its letters, here its back half
both says the cut applies to each of the two girls alike

parts.note: lasses are girls, here taken as a pair of them
the second half of girl

explanation.surface: Gaston watches the girls he dates, both of them a bit tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-cut', British slang for tipsy, here halves each GIRL to GI, and 'both' means it happens twice. Gaston is the suitor in Colette's novella, later the musical film.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigi is the title heroine of Colette's novella, loved by the wealthy Gaston who finally marries her.

clue.text: When the queen turned on article, then the PM?

indicators.note: on means placed after, the next piece in the line

parts.note: the definite article

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, read backwards

parts.note: as can mean when, as in as I left
ER is Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A question about when a monarch rounded on someone and then on a prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When' is also MAY: Theresa followed by MAY gives the British Prime Minister in office when the puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: Theresa May was UK Prime Minister from 2016 to 2019; her forename plus a word for when names her.

clue.text: Ridiculously moronic character of Euripides

indicators.note: something done ridiculously is absurd and disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A foolish figure in a Greek tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a role in a play, but it is a letter of the alphabet Euripides wrote in.
explanation.definitionFit: Omicron is a letter of the Greek alphabet, and a written letter is called a character.

clue.text: "Lolita, –, fire of my loins. My sin, my soul." (Vladimir Nabokov)

definitions.text: "Lolita, –, fire of my loins. My sin, my soul." (Vladimir Nabokov)

parts.words: "Lolita, –, fire of my loins. My sin, my soul." (Vladimir Nabokov)
parts.note: the surface reading: a line of prose with a gap; the setter's reading: the gap is filled from the famous opening sentence of Nabokov's novel

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue with no wordplay: the solver must recall the first words of Nabokov's Lolita, spoken by the narrator Humbert Humbert.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing phrase begins the novel, published in 1955, in which Humbert addresses his obsession directly.
